newsitem.title: JAPAN: Tokyo says Taiwan covered by U.S.-Japan pact.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo says Taiwan covered by U.S.-Japan pact.

text.p: Japan's top government spokesman said on Tuesday that a bilateral security review with the United States covers possible conflicts across the Taiwan Strait as well as the Korean Peninsula.

Since last year, Tokyo and Washington have been reviewing their 1978 "Guidelines for Defence Cooperation", which include provisions for Japan to support the U.S. military in regional conflicts under the treaty.

"The 'Far East' covered in the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty covers the area north of the Philippines...that includes the Taiwan Strait and the Korean peninsula," Chief Cabinet Secretary Seiroku Kajiyama told a news conference.
"I am not aware that the revision includes a change in the fundamentals of the security pact," Kajiyama said.
China has repeatedly warned Japan not to include Taiwan as a region covered under the review of the guidelines of the U.S.-Japan Security Treaty.
In an interim report on the review of guidelines announced in June, the two governments did not specify a geographical limit to be covered.
The interim report says Japan might send warships to take part in U.N.-sanctioned naval blockades and minesweeping operations during an armed conflict "surrounding Japan".
A final report is due in September.
On Sunday, Kajiyama made similar remarks about the review of the guidelines in a television talk show, drawing sharp criticism from China.
Referring to Kajiyama's remarks, China's official Xinhua news agency said on Monday: "It threatens China's sovereignty and safety, and it obviously calls for a high degree of precaution."
Two U.S. Navy aircraft carriers were sent to waters near Taiwan in March 1996 after China conducted missile tests and war games during Taiwan's presidential elections.
Kajiyama's latest remarks come ahead of a planned visit by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to China next month.

China, which suffered under Japanese invasion and occupation in the 1930s and 1940s, has long seen the possibility of any change in Tokyo's officially passive defence policy as a possible revival of World War Two-style militarism.
Japan's pacifist constitution bars it from settling international disputes by military means.

In June, Tokyo sent envoys to China to soothe Beijing's concerns over the proposed revisions to the guidelines, which are expected to give Japan its highest military profile in Asia since World War Two.
